content: Palliative care has the potential to alleviate pain and unnecessary suffering for millions of cancer patients worldwide, provided they have timely access to quality care. This module outlines the development of effective palliative care programs within the framework of national cancer control initiatives. It builds upon the comprehensive planning module for cancer control, which provides a detailed understanding of the overall planning process. While this module focuses on cancer, it acknowledges the importance of a public health approach to palliative care that addresses the needs of individuals of all ages suffering from various conditions requiring such care. These conditions include HIV/AIDS, congestive heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, neurodegenerative disorders, chronic respiratory diseases, and illnesses associated with aging. The principles guiding palliative care development for cancer patients are similar to those for other chronic diseases. In 2005, six million people died from cancer, and without intervention, 84 million more are projected to die in the next decade. Over 70% of cancer deaths occur in lowand middle-income countries, where resources for prevention, diagnosis, and treatment are often limited or unavailable. However, cancer is largely preventable, with over 40% of cases being avoidable. Many common cancers are curable if detected early and treated appropriately. Even in advanced stages, patients' suffering can be alleviated through effective palliative care. The Cancer Control: Knowledge into Action series by the World Health Organization (WHO) provides guidance on all critical aspects of cancer control, including prevention, early detection, diagnosis, treatment, and palliative care. This series emphasizes the importance of evidence-based interventions to reduce cancer incidence, morbidity, and mortality while improving the quality of life for patients. Comprehensive cancer control programs should address the entire population while catering to the specific needs of at-risk subgroups. Palliative care is particularly crucial in low-resource settings, where many patients are diagnosed at advanced stages when curative treatment is no longer effective. These patients can benefit significantly from low-cost interventions that relieve suffering. Effective palliative care services should be integrated into existing healthcare systems at all levels, with a focus on community and home-based care. These services must be culturally, socially, and economically appropriate for the specific setting. They should also be strategically linked to cancer prevention, early detection, and treatment services for both adults and children. Palliative care should begin at the time of diagnosis of a life-threatening illness and adapt to the increasing needs of patients and their families as the disease progresses. It should also provide bereavement support to families. Palliative care improves the quality of life for patients and their families by addressing physical, psychological, social, and spiritual needs. It provides relief from pain and other distressing symptoms, affirms life while recognizing dying as a natural process, and neither hastens nor postpones death. It supports patients in living as actively as possible until death and helps families cope during the illness and bereavement periods. Palliative care is applicable early in the course of illness, alongside treatments intended to prolong life, such as chemotherapy or radiation therapy. The story of Subair, a 50-year-old cancer patient in India, illustrates the transformative impact of good palliative care. After undergoing multiple surgeries, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy, Subair faced severe pain and financial hardship, which led to his children being placed in an orphanage. Seeking relief, he visited a palliative care clinic where he was prescribed oral morphine, which provided complete pain relief. With effective pain management, Subair regained his independence, found employment, and was able to reunite with and support his family. Over the years, despite disease progression and increased morphine doses, Subair has remained pain-free and active, ensuring his children’s education and celebrating life milestones. His story exemplifies the profound benefits of quality palliative care. In conclusion, palliative care is an urgent humanitarian need for individuals with cancer and other chronic, life-threatening illnesses.
